title: 5,000-Year-Old Wolves on a Baltic Island Weren't There by Accident
hook: Wolf remains on a tiny Swedish island — with no native land mammals and no way to swim there — mean humans brought them, fed them, and maybe even nursed an injured one back to health.
key_points: Wolf remains dated to 3,000–5,000 years ago were found on Stora Karlsö, a small Baltic island off Sweden with no native land mammals.
Since wolves couldn't have reached the isolated island naturally, humans must have transported them there by boat.
Isotope analysis shows the wolves ate large amounts of marine protein — seals and fish — matching the human diet on the island, suggesting deliberate feeding.
The island's wolves were smaller than mainland wolves, and one showed unusually low genetic diversity, patterns typical of isolated or managed populations.
One Bronze Age wolf had severe limb damage that would have prevented hunting, yet survived — implying it received care.
content_html: Wolf bones don't belong on a tiny, isolated Baltic island with no native land mammals — unless someone brought them there. That's exactly what researchers found on Stora Karlsö, and the evidence suggests those wolves were doing more than surviving on their own.
extra_html: Dated to 3,000–5,000 years ago, the island's wolves show a chemical signature — heavy in marine protein from seals and fish — that closely tracks the diet of the humans living there, pointing to deliberate feeding rather than independent foraging. They were also smaller than mainland wolves, and one showed unusually low genetic diversity, a pattern typical of small, human-managed populations. Most striking is a Bronze Age wolf with limb damage severe enough to prevent hunting, which nonetheless survived — hard to explain unless people cared for it. Rather than domestication happening only once, gradually, on the path to dogs, this suggests prehistoric communities experimented with managing wolves in their own right, a "forgotten chapter" of the long, complicated relationship between humans and wild canines.

related.title: Human Evolution
related.hook: We didn't descend from chimpanzees — we share an ancestor with them. From that branching point, our lineage walked upright, grew big brains, and spread across the planet.

related.title: Natural Selection
related.hook: No designer, no goal — just heritable variation, a struggle to survive, and the slow accumulation of whatever happens to work. That's how life adapts.

flashcards.prompt: Why must humans have brought these wolves to the Baltic island?
flashcards.back_html: The island, Stora Karlsö, has no native land mammals and is cut off by open sea — wolves couldn't have swum or walked there. They must have arrived by boat, brought by people.

flashcards.prompt: What evidence suggests these wolves were deliberately fed by humans?

choices.text: Isotope analysis shows they ate large amounts of marine protein matching the human diet on the island
Their bones were found buried alongside dog bones
Ancient writings describe the practice directly

flashcards.explanation_html: Chemical isotope signatures in the wolves' bones closely matched the marine-heavy diet (seals and fish) that people on the island ate, pointing to deliberate feeding rather than the wolves foraging on their own.

flashcards.prompt: What does the injured Bronze Age wolf's survival suggest?

choices.text: It likely received care from humans, since its injury would have prevented it from hunting on its own
Wolves can fully regenerate damaged limbs naturally
The injury had no effect on the wolf's ability to survive

flashcards.explanation_html: With limb damage severe enough to prevent hunting, the wolf's survival is hard to explain without some form of human support or care.
